newsitem.title: USA: Snow-coated N.Dakota readies for inevitable floods.
newsitem.headline: Snow-coated N.Dakota readies for inevitable floods.

text.p: Circled by a dike made of suitcase-sized chunks of rich, black earth dug from the Red River Valley, the village of Harwood, along with many others in North Dakota, waited Wednesday for a flood.
It may be three weeks away but it could be the worst in 100 years in a floodplain that runs north into Canada's prairies and out to Hudson Bay.

For months Harwood's 590 residents have been preoccupied with winter. Even under a warm early spring sun, snow was still piled roof-high in front of many homes and driveways ran into garages through canyons cut through snow from the streets and sidewalks.
The earthen dike encircling Harwood, about seven feet tall and wide, runs along streets and through backyards. It may be extended across the interstate highway if water reaches that far.

The realisation that the snow will soon become torrents of water "is just beginning to hit now that it's warming up," said Jennifer Arndt, a waitress at the Conoco truck stop on Interstate 29 in Harwood, a few miles north of Fargo.

The Sheyenne River, which forecasters have said will crest three feet higher than ever recorded just outside Harwwood, was lightly etched in the snow and ice, more a brook than a river. Three miles east of Harwood, the Red River, into which the Sheyenne flows, was only a meandering stream in a shallow, wooded valley, the vast farm fields still hidden by snow.
But topography and a record snowfall in the basin appear bound to collide.

Fargo, at only 900 feet above sea level, is near the top of the Red River Valley that borders Canada. The river itself has not dug a deep valley in its relatively young geological life and floodwaters will likely spread far and wide, turning thousands of acres between Fargo and Winnepeg, Manitoba, into lakes.

Larger cities such as Fargo and Grand Forks were shoring up flood protection systems built after previous bouts with high water. Winnipeg, experts believe, is safe behind a diversion system built after a 1950 flood.
Greg Wiche of the United States Geological Service believes this year's flood could the the worst since the Red River flood of 1897 caused major damage to Grand Forks and other communities.

Farmers said they were worried about delayed spring planting for wheat and other crops and plumbers said they had all the work they could handle removing basement toilets and sealing off the pipes. The Fargo Forum newspaper was full of flood preparation advertising: sandbags filled, $1 each, minimum order 100; backhoe available to dike homes and farms, and of course snow removal.
Students at Moorhead State University in Minnesota across the river from Fargo filled sandbags Tuesday to protect some of the school's operating plants.

Farther upriver, Wahpeton in North Dakota and Breckenridge across the river in Minnesota were squabbling over dike-building. Breckenridge claimed a line of sandbags Wahpeton wants to lay to protect its zoo and other park property would push flood water into Minnesota. Some of the animals meanwhile were being moved to other zoos for safekeeping.
North Dakota Gov. Ed Schafer has declared seven counties disaster areas and was preparing to do the same for others.
